These definitions concern the specified measure. On a probability space,
convergence in measure is called convergence in probability.
text:
On a space of finite measure, a.e.\ convergence implies convergence in
measure and not conversely; without finiteness the implication fails.
These comparisons are proved in \cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-005-ae-measure}.

anchor_quote:
Apply the finite construction on each \(D_m\), with its trace sigma-algebra.
It gives a measurable density \(h_m\) there and a residual \(\sigma_m\)
concentrated on \(A_m\subseteq D_m\), where \(\mu(A_m)=0\).
Extend each density by zero outside \(D_m\) and set
\[
 g=\sum_mh_m\mathbf1_{D_m},\quad
 \nu_{\mathrm r}(E)=\int_Eg\,d\mu,\quad
 \nu_{\mathrm s}(E)=\sum_m\sigma_m(E\cap D_m).
\]
The piecewise function is measurable. Countable additivity and
nonnegative integral summation give
\(\nu_{\mathrm r}(E)+\nu_{\mathrm s}(E)=\sum_m\nu(E\cap D_m)=\nu(E)\).
This assembly never subtracts two infinite values.
The union \(A=\bigcup_mA_m\) has \(\mu(A)=0\) and
\(\nu_{\mathrm s}(A^c)=0\).
Also \(\int_{D_m}g\,d\mu\leq\nu(D_m)<\infty\), so \(g\) is finite
almost everywhere on every \(D_m\), and hence on \(\Omega\).
text:
Apply the finite construction on each nonempty \(D_m\), on the measure
space \((D_m,\mathcal F_{D_m},\mu|_{D_m})\) with the finite measure
\(\nu|_{D_m}\), in the notation of
\cref{def:p15-w02c-p15-003-trace-sigma-field}; by part~(2) of
\cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-003-trace-generation} these are finite measures
on the trace sigma-algebra \(\mathcal F_{D_m}=\{B\in\mathcal F:B\subseteq D_m\}\).
It gives an \(\mathcal F_{D_m}\)-measurable \(h_m:D_m\to[0,\infty]\),
the measure \(\rho_m(B)=\int_Bh_m\,d(\mu|_{D_m})\) on
\(\mathcal F_{D_m}\), and a residual \(\sigma_m=\nu|_{D_m}-\rho_m\)
concentrated on some \(A_m\in\mathcal F_{D_m}\) with \(\mu(A_m)=0\).
For an empty \(D_m\) put \(h_m\), \(\rho_m\), \(\sigma_m\) equal to zero
and \(A_m=\varnothing\).
Let \(\bar h_m\) be the zero extension of \(h_m\) to \(\Omega\), and set
\[
 g=\sum_m\bar h_m,\quad
 \nu_{\mathrm r}(E)=\int_Eg\,d\mu,\quad
 \nu_{\mathrm s}(E)=\sum_m\sigma_m(E\cap D_m).
\]
Each \(\bar h_m\) is \(\mathcal F\)-measurable by part~(1) of
\cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-003-block-integrals}, so \(g\), a sum of
nonnegative measurable functions, is measurable; since the blocks are
disjoint, \(g=h_m\) on \(D_m\). Fix \(E\in\mathcal F\). Term-by-term
integration of the nonnegative series \(\mathbf1_Eg=\sum_m\mathbf1_E\bar h_m\)
(\cref{thm:p15-nonnegative-integral-laws}) gives
\(\nu_{\mathrm r}(E)=\sum_m\int\mathbf1_E\bar h_m\,d\mu\).
The function \(\mathbf1_E\bar h_m\) is the zero extension of the
\(\mathcal F_{D_m}\)-measurable function \(\mathbf1_{E\cap D_m}h_m\) on
\(D_m\), so part~(1) of \cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-003-block-integrals},
applied to the measure \(\mu\), identifies its integral over \(\Omega\)
against \(\mu\) with the integral on \(D_m\) against \(\mu|_{D_m}\):
\[
 \int\mathbf1_E\bar h_m\,d\mu
   =\int_{D_m}\mathbf1_{E\cap D_m}h_m\,d(\mu|_{D_m})
   =\rho_m(E\cap D_m).
\]
Hence \(\nu_{\mathrm r}(E)=\sum_m\rho_m(E\cap D_m)\), and adding the
residuals term by term, all terms being nonnegative,
\(\nu_{\mathrm r}(E)+\nu_{\mathrm s}(E)=\sum_m\nu(E\cap D_m)=\nu(E)\)
by countable additivity of \(\nu\). Both \(\nu_{\mathrm r}\) and
\(\nu_{\mathrm s}\) are measures on \(\mathcal F\): the first is an
indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function, and the second
is a countable sum of the measures \(E\mapsto\sigma_m(E\cap D_m)\).
This assembly never subtracts two infinite values.
The union \(A=\bigcup_mA_m\) lies in \(\mathcal F\) and has
\(\mu(A)=0\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm s}(A^c)=0\), because
\(\sigma_m(A^c\cap D_m)=\sigma_m(D_m\setminus A_m)=0\) for every \(m\).
Taking \(E=D_m\) above gives
\(\int_{D_m}g\,d\mu=\rho_m(D_m)\leq\nu(D_m)<\infty\), so \(g\) is finite
almost everywhere on every \(D_m\), and hence on \(\Omega\).

The replacement supplies that step by part (1) of thm:p15-w02c-p15-003-block-integrals (proved in annex:p15-w02c-p15-003-block-integrals, chapter of packet w02ca-p15-003, which must be routed before radon-nikodym or at least in the same build) and term-by-term integration of nonnegative series, and makes measurability of the zero extensions, the measure property of nu_s and the null-set bookkeeping explicit.

For a two-point law with \(\mathbb P(X=x)=\lambda\) and
\(\mathbb P(X=y)=1-\lambda\), the inequality is the defining inequality
of convexity. This illustration, which Durrett gives with his
Theorem~1.6.2, and his Figure~1.6, for \(g(x)=x^2-3x+3\) with
\(\mathbb P(X=1)=\mathbb P(X=3)=1/2\), are worked in
\cref{def:p15-w02c-p15-005-jensen-direction}
\cite[thm.~1.6.2 and fig.~1.6, pp.~29--30]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}; the
special cases \(|\mathbb EX|\leq\mathbb E|X|\) and
\((\mathbb EX)^2\leq\mathbb E(X^2)\) that he names there are
\cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-005-jensen-special}. What each hypothesis of the
theorem does is shown in \cref{sec:p15-w02c-p15-001-jensen-hypotheses}:
the total mass one cannot be dropped on a finite measure space, infinite
total mass does not decide the inequality, integrability of
\(\varphi(f)\) can be dropped by reading the right side as an extended
integral, and integrability of \(f\) cannot be dropped.
